title: CPA firm plans family-office accounting modernisation on an AI-driven multi-entity platform
problem: Multi-entity family offices keep accounting, investment reporting and operations in separate tools and spreadsheets, so closing and consolidating take manual effort and reporting is hard to trust.
approach: Announced: PKF O'Connor Davies plans to leverage the Asseta AI platform for family offices, from evaluation and implementation through ongoing financial operations.
The release does not say the firm already runs any family's books on it; the vendor says it reconciles inter-company accounts automatically.
Vendor says most family offices go live in 8-12 weeks, and claims $125B+ assets and 50+ families onboarded (vendor-published).
Per the vendor's plan, historical data reconciliation is finished and the team trained before go-live.

title: AI extraction of alternative-investment documents into one system of record
problem: Capital calls, distributions, valuation statements and K-1s arrive in each fund manager's own format, and staff re-key them into spreadsheets and reconcile by hand.
approach: A document-AI module ingests the PDFs, identifies key data points and posts a reviewable draft to the family office's reporting platform.
A person reviews the extracted draft before it is posted; capital-call funding instructions are checked against procedure.
At Jefferson River Capital, Masttro's Doc AI automated data capture for capital calls, distributions and valuations.
The implementation enabled tracking of 200+ alternative investments; no time or error figures are published (vendor-published).
who: Masttro, Jefferson River Capital, Armanino, Canoe

title: AI-drafted reporting commentary and consolidated multi-entity reports for principals
problem: Investment reporting is still too manual, and families expect consolidated views across entities, investments and cash without waiting weeks for someone to stitch them together.
approach: Staff use AI to draft reporting commentary, summarize documents and prepare meeting material; platforms consolidate entity-level numbers into one view.
A person signs off on AI-drafted commentary and reports; final decisions, especially on investments, stay with experienced humans.
Survey: 16% of family offices use AI for investment performance reporting, more than double a year earlier (vendor-published).
73% of survey respondents still find investment reporting too manual (vendor-published).
who: Armanino, Citi, RBC with Campden Wealth, UBS

title: AI help with transaction coding, reconciliation and month-end close in family-office accounting
problem: Lean teams code transactions, reconcile accounts across entities and banks, and run the close by hand across fragmented systems.
approach: AI categorizes invoices and transactions, reconciles accounts across entities and banks, and flags anomalies; a person reviews the exceptions.
Sources name this as where practitioners are trying AI; one family office's controller posting asks the hire to assess AI-assisted tooling.
Armanino keeps moving money, posting to the books and final decisions with people, who sign off on AI-prepared work.
No family-office outcome is published; an adjacent small-business study links generative AI to faster month-end closing, no figure given (independent).

title: General-purpose AI assistants for family-office staff on ad hoc operations tasks
problem: Small family-office teams lack specialist skills (for example Salesforce development) and lose time on low-value conversion and admin work.
approach: Staff use AI assistants directly, with no workflow around them; no review step is described in the sources.
Ford Estates LLC's investment operations director says assistants got the office reasonably close to the code needed for Salesforce automations.
Placements Italcan Inc. uses AI to convert Excel files to formats its software needs and to manage trips and travel costs.
The office built Salesforce automations without in-house deep Salesforce experience; no time or cost figure given (self-reported).
who: Ford Estates LLC, Placements Italcan Inc.

title: AI comparison of limited partner agreement language in fund due diligence
problem: Family-office staff read and compare long limited partner (LP) agreements and other fund documents during due diligence.
approach: Staff use AI to validate comparisons within LP agreements, compare standard against new language and support due diligence.
Placements Italcan Inc.'s CEO describes this use; Wingspan reports practitioners comparing contract language and pressure-testing LP agreements.
Counsel or the responsible executive reviews anything relied on; investment selection itself is out of scope.
Use is self-reported only; no outcome figures are published.

title: AI flagging of payment anomalies alongside procedural controls against deepfake fraud
problem: AI-generated voice, video and writing make payment requests look authentic; family offices are lean, rely on informal channels and are likely targets.
approach: Announced: software flags anomalies in payments and approvals and discrepancies in wiring information.
The office adds procedural controls, dual authorization and verification outside the request channel, because detection tools lag attackers.
Canoe lists proactive flagging of wiring-information discrepancies as a platform feature; no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).

title: AI platform coordinating a multidisciplinary family-office service team
problem: Delivering the resources of a family office through individual advisors means coordinating many services, systems and specialists per family.
approach: Mercer Advisors' Aspen is a unified knowledge graph mapping relationships between clients, advisory teams and services across planning, custody and productivity systems.
Second generation unveiled in July 2026; the company says it is deployed across more than 1,100 wealth professionals (self-reported).
The company says it powers hundreds of thousands of actions a year and serves 42,000+ clients (self-reported).
No review step is described; only the coordination step is counted, not regulated advice or tax preparation.

title: AI agents preparing advisor follow-ups and service tickets from the client record
problem: Advisors serving complex families spend time on meeting follow-up and routine requests rather than on the relationship.
approach: Announced: Compound Planning's CompoundAI agents draw on holdings, meeting transcripts and communication history to prepare work for advisor review.
A General Assistant agent summarizes recent activity and drafts follow-up emails and agendas.
A Service Request agent turns tasks, such as a gift of appreciated stock to a donor-advised fund, into a ticket for sign-off.
Advisors review and sign off drafts and tickets; no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).

title: Live consolidated family view with AI summaries and natural-language access for principals
problem: Principals and heirs expect timely, app-like access to a single view of entities, investments and cash, not periodic static PDFs.
approach: Platforms consolidate data across custodians and entities and add AI summaries and assistants; advisors position live reporting as replacing periodic packages.
Masttro lists AI-powered wealth intelligence and a family communication portal; Asseta lists dashboard analytics and forecasting.
Relationship managers keep judgment and client contact.
No outcome figures are published; the case rests on principals' expectations (vendor-published).
who: Masttro, Asseta, Armanino, Kaufman Rossin, Wiss

title: Idea: AI capturing institutional knowledge to reduce key-person risk in family offices
problem: Idea, not a deployment: much of how a family office runs lives in a few people's heads, so reports depend on who knows which entity owns what.
approach: Idea only: practitioners discuss AI helping capture and surface institutional knowledge, as a continuity tool as much as a productivity tool (Armanino).
No deployment found, no outcome figures published, and no human checkpoint described.

title: Idea: AI scenario modelling and successor assessment in family-business succession advice
problem: Idea, not a deployment: family-business succession carries emotional and business risk, and many families have no plan.
approach: Idea only: an advisor would use predictive analytics and simulation to model succession scenarios and assess candidates' leadership potential from performance data.
The FFI Practitioner article names general commercial tools; no source shows them used in a family-succession engagement.
UBS found fewer than a third of family offices with a succession plan consulted the next generation at the outset.
The article assumes advisors remain responsible; no review step is described.

title: Idea: AI-supported exit-readiness conversations with business-owner clients
problem: Idea, not a deployment: owner exits depend on leadership alignment, decision-making and institutional knowledge, and advisors want ways to start early AI conversations with owners.
approach: Idea only: Certified Exit Planning Advisors guide owners on how AI affects enterprise value and exit readiness, making gaps visible.
An Exit Planning Institute webinar page frames this as a people-side question and promises examples and a framework; no results given.

title: Advising families on AI policy, data limits and vendor diligence
problem: Family offices handle the most sensitive data of any client and adopt AI tools without a policy; leaks can occur through ordinary use with no breach event.
approach: Announced: banks, law firms and CPA firms publish AI policy templates; whether any sells this as a paid service is not shown.
They advise inventorying AI use cases, tiering them by risk, approving tools, vetting vendors and training staff; Northern Trust gives ten principles.
AI output is reviewed before reliance, especially on investment, legal, tax and estate matters; policy is reviewed at least annually.
Squire Patton Boggs gives a six-part governance response; Armanino and Wiss advise setting data and review rules before adoption.
who: Northern Trust, Squire Patton Boggs, Armanino, Wiss

title: Hybrid family-office model: outsourced accounting and AI enablement, strategy kept in-house
problem: Lean offices lack bandwidth to build and maintain a bench for each of accounting, reporting, technology, AI and security.
approach: Offices keep strategy, family relationships and decisions in-house and move accounting, reporting, technology, AI enablement and cybersecurity to outside providers.
Armanino describes this as the trend; PKF's Asseta collaboration is the nearest named example.
GenTrust's CIO says family offices have asked it to find staff who can find AI technology to automate bill pay and concierge.
Armanino, citing Campden Wealth and AlTi Tiedemann Global (2025), says 80% outsource mainly for expertise, 31% for cost savings (vendor-published).

title: AI-assisted cash-flow modelling from family-office profit-and-loss history
problem: A family office's board asks for a model of monthly cash flow, which would otherwise be built by hand from years of profit-and-loss statements.
approach: Joshua S. Miller, CEO of Minot's Light Management, used Copilot to review five years of monthly P&L statements and chart total expenses.
He then used Copilot in Excel to chart actual monthly cash flow and averages to model future cash flow.
The CEO edited the output and spot-checked the numbers.
Estimate: work that would likely have taken hours took about 45 minutes, including editing and spot checks (self-reported).

title: Client-facing custom GPT answering basic succession questions for family-held businesses
problem: A firm helping family-held businesses prepare for leadership transition wants a way to start conversations with its target audience before they are ready to meet.
approach: GWCPA, a CPA firm in La Plata, Maryland, built the 'GWCPA Generations Advisor', a customized ChatGPT deployment advising on ownership transitions.
Its marketing partner wrote the instructions and uploaded the firm's marketing materials; access comes by joining the firm's free email list.
Deeper conversations happen with the firm team when the prospect is ready to meet.
The marketing partner attributes about 50 new mailing-list members in three months to it (self-reported).
